summary.title: Individuals matter
summary.one_liner: Moving or abandoning people on a team destroys institutional knowledge and culture, and management incentives that reward headcount or ignore individual contribution cause predictable harm.
keywords: promotion based on number of reports
comms pr approval for engineering blog posts
takeaways: Reassigning a team against its wishes can cause senior people to quit and destroy the team's institutional knowledge and culture, which is hard to rebuild.
Managers who are rewarded by how many people report to them have an incentive to collect headcount rather than value individual contribution.
Bureaucratic approval processes protect against rare downside risks but cost companies the upside of bold moves and public engineering writing.
Claimed project wins often exceed measured results, and some A/B test setups can produce spurious wins.
Location-based pay adjustments can cause employees to leave, and companies with small adjustments can hire away people from those with large ones.
summary.summary: This is a personal essay by Dan Luu arguing that individuals matter in tech organizations. It opens with anecdotes of teams that collapsed after being reassigned or having priorities abruptly reversed, then discusses how managers can be incentivized to accumulate headcount and how bureaucracy suppresses valuable work. The essay also looks at overstated claimed wins and at location-based pay adjustments, which the author says drive employees to leave. It is written as opinion and anecdote, with links to related essays and a few cited ideas from Yossi Kreinin and James C. Scott, rather than as a how-to guide.
